stem: In which states of matter can convection happen?

options.content: Liquids and gases only
Solids only
Solids, liquids and gases
Gases only

explanation: Convection needs the material to flow, so it happens only in fluids (liquids and gases).

options.content: Heat always rises, carrying the warm air up with it.
options.rationale: It is the warm, less dense air that rises.

options.content: Warm air has fewer particles in total, so it weighs less.
It expands, becomes less dense and is pushed up by cooler air.
Warm air is attracted upwards by the heat of the Sun.

explanation: Heated air expands, so its density decreases; cooler, denser air sinks around it and pushes it upwards.

stem: Why is the heating element of an electric kettle at the bottom?

options.content: So that the element itself stays cool in the water.
Because heat sinks, so it would not reach the bottom water.
Heated water rises, so a convection current heats all the water.
So that the water can conduct the heat upwards quickly.
options.rationale: Water is a poor conductor; convection does the job.

explanation: Warm water rises from the element and cooler water sinks to be heated: convection circulates all the water.

stem: An air conditioner works best mounted high on a wall, because cool air sinks.
explanation: The cooled air is denser, so it sinks through the room, setting up a convection current.

stem: A learner drops a crystal of potassium permanganate to the bottom of a beaker of water, near one side, and heats the beaker gently under that side.

points.description: A purple stream rises from above the crystal on the heated side
It spreads across the top, sinks on the far side and returns along the bottom (a circulating current)
The water above the flame is heated and expands
so it becomes less dense and rises
cooler, denser water sinks to replace it, setting up a convection current

explanation: Heated water expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler water sinks; the coloured stream traces the convection current.
hints: What happens to the density of water when it is heated?

stem: Where should the cooling unit of an old-style refrigerator be placed, and why?

options.content: At the bottom: cold air rises and cools the whole fridge.
In the middle: the position does not matter for cooling.
Outside the fridge, so that its own heat does not warm the food
At the top: cooled air sinks, and warmer air rises to be cooled.

explanation: Air cooled at the top becomes denser and sinks, while warmer air rises to the cooling unit: a convection current cools the whole interior.
hints: Does cold air rise or sink?

stem: Why does a hot-air balloon rise?

options.content: Hot air is lighter because the heating has destroyed some of its particles.
options.rationale: It has the same particles, spread out.

options.content: The heated air inside is less dense than the cooler air outside.
The burner pushes it up like a rocket.
The balloon's fabric is lighter than air.

explanation: Air inside the balloon expands when heated; the balloon's average density falls below that of the surrounding air.
